newsitem.title: RUSSIA: AGROKHLEB - Russia 1997 spring sowing starts early.
newsitem.headline: AGROKHLEB - Russia 1997 spring sowing starts early.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from SovEcon Ltd, an independent research organisation specialising in agricultural production and trade in the former Soviet Union.
RUSSIA: 1997 SPRING FIELD WORK AHEAD OF 1996 DESPITE CONSTRAINTS
In Russia, spring field work has started under input shortages and severe financial constraints.
But despite the problems, the 1997 spring grain planting campaign has started earlier than last year.
An area of 460,000 hectares in Russia had been sown to spring grains by April 7, 25 percent up on year-ago levels.

According to SovEcon's early estimates, potential maximum grain output in Russia can be evaluated at a relatively low 80 million tonnes, even with favourable growing conditions, because of the shortage of pedigree seeds and the lack of financing.
By the beginning of field works, about one third of agricultural machinery was still not in working order.

The problem was exacerbated by extremely low stocks of fuel at farms. And in contrast to last year, the Russian government has left a barter scheme which had provided farmers with fuel for agricultural commodities.
Instead of cheap commodity credits, the government has established a special fund of 2.8 trillion roubles for crediting season field work in 1997.
The Finance Ministry was supposed to have made the total payment to Agroprombank by March 31, but the first installment of 336 billion roubles only just arrived in the bank's account.
The Food and Agriculture Ministry therefore had to ask some commercial banks to provide credits.
Alfa-bank, which is now entitled to service the fund alongside Agroprombank, had allocated one trillion roubles for the special fund as of April 9.

NOTE - The 1996 spring campaign lagged well behind the normal pace, so current spring grain planting progress is slightly behind normal as well.
However, reseeded winter plantings area is negligible so far. It accounts for only 0.7 percent of the total compared with 1.4 percent at the same data last year.
It is a strong indicator of reduced winterkill losses in the North Caucasus, Russia's wheat belt, this year.
